suggestions.quote: Your room papered with every page you have read, and the crimson shout from age nine following you into the kitchen, talking over the tea she just brought
suggestions.fix: She sets the chai down. You throw the shout from when you were nine back at her. She doesn't remember it at all. I already had the pages, the shout and the cup in the first seven seconds; this is where I leave.

suggestions.quote: The second fact, about the people who live this: people who remember almost every day of their lives, and Jill Price's own words about it
suggestions.fix: You snap at her over that old shout. She doesn't remember it. One line of Jill Price's, on her blank face: the past never gets quiet. Cut the second finding so two facts don't land while I wait.

suggestions.quote: At eighty, the shout from age nine is as loud as this morning, and so is the morning she taught you to ride a cycle.
suggestions.fix: At eighty the morning she taught you to ride a cycle is as loud as the shout, and you choose which one speaks tonight. I already know the shout never fades.

suggestions.quote: the tea already in her hand
suggestions.fix: the chai already in her hand (same cup in the kitchen beat and in "Mom brings tea")

suggestions.quote: whether you are still found first on both themes is the cold read (K1, K2), in the room notes below.

keep.quote: you'll forget it all after anyway
you can't lose the shout, but you can stop replaying it
when someone tells you they forgot, it may be the kindest thing they did
